sha256:19d9a516c9e6645d9158a9059df774f6c.body:
On Thursday (#412) the response cache's index, a `std::unordered_map<int, int>`, was replaced with an open-addressing table. The map allocated one heap node per insert, about 9% of CPU at peak; the table allocates nothing per request. CPU at peak is down 9%, but since the deploy:

- the cache hit ratio went from **94.1%** to **71.3%**, worst on the PoPs that purge the most;
- origin requests are up **3.2×**;
- `edgectl cache get` reports misses for keys whose responses are visibly in the arena.

```text
14:02:11 purge key=3                        ok
14:02:19 get   key=11  miss                 (arena slot 4: key=11, age 41s)
14:02:19 get   key=19  miss                 (arena slot 5: key=19, age 38s)
```

Fix the index without giving up the flat table.

## The table

- A flat array of `slots` slots, allocated once when the index is created. `slots` is 0 or more.
- A key's home slot is `key % slots` (keys are already hashes, used as unsigned); on a collision, the next slot, wrapping around at the end (linear probing).
- A lookup walks from the home slot until it finds the key or reaches an empty slot.

## What to write

`cache_index(slots, ops)` replays a cache log against a new index of `slots` slots and returns what each get found, in order, `-1` for a miss. Each op is one of:

- `["put", key, value]`: store `value` (0 or more) under `key`, replacing any value already stored under it;
- `["get", key]`: look `key` up;
- `["erase", key]`: purge `key`, if it is stored (purging a key that is not stored does nothing).

The index must behave like a map of at most `slots` entries:

- A get finds the latest value put under its key, unless the key was purged since; otherwise it is a miss.
- A purged response must never come back.
- A put of a key that is already stored always succeeds. A put of a new key is refused (the response is served uncached, and later gets miss) only when every slot holds a live entry; slots freed by purges must be usable again.

## Constraints

- Keep the flat table, allocation-free: no node-based or heap containers (`std::map`, `std::unordered_map`, `std::set`, `std::unordered_set`, `std::list`), no `new`, and no `make_unique` or `make_shared`.

rules.message: The index must stay an allocation-free flat table: no std::map, std::unordered_map, std::set, std::unordered_set or std::list, no new and no make_unique or make_shared.

The cart drawer and the header badge show whatever `Cart.summary()` returns. To keep the drawer fast, `summary()` was memoised: the drawer calls it on every render, and repricing a 60-line cart each time cost 38 ms a frame (now about 2). Since then the drawer sometimes shows an old total. A shopper's report:

> I changed the jeans from 1 to 2 in my cart and it still said $59.00. Then checkout charged me $118.00.

Removing an item shows the right total; changing a quantity doesn't. Make every `summary()` reflect the cart as it is at that moment, and keep the memo.

**What `summary()` returns.** `{ items, subtotal, discount, total }`, amounts in whole cents: `items` is the sum of the lines' quantities, `subtotal` the sum of `price × quantity`, `discount` the promo code's discount on the subtotal, and `total` is `subtotal − discount`.

**The cart.**

- `add(sku, price, quantity = 1)` adds that quantity to the line with that SKU, or adds a new line `{ sku, price, quantity }` if there is none. Adding to an existing line keeps the line's price.
- `setQuantity(sku, quantity)` sets a line's quantity; 0 or less removes the line. It does nothing for a SKU not in the cart.
- `remove(sku)` removes the line.
- `applyCode(code)` sets the promo code: `{ name, percent }`, `{ name, amount }` (in cents), or `null` to remove it. Two codes can share a name and differ in what they take off.

**Discounts.** `discountFor(code, subtotal)`, imported from `./discounts.js`, is 0 without a code; a percent code takes `Math.round(subtotal × percent / 100)`, an amount code takes its amount, and the discount is never more than the subtotal. `sum(amounts)`, imported from `./money.js`, adds up an array of numbers.

**The memo stays.** `summary()` must not reprice the cart when nothing changed since the last call. Keep the result cached in a field on the cart named for what it does (the starter's `this.cache`, or for example a version number or a dirty flag) rather than taking the memo out.

**Tests.** `replay(actions)` plays a session on a new cart and returns what `summary()` showed each time it was asked. Actions are `["add", sku, price, quantity?]`, `["quantity", sku, quantity]`, `["remove", sku]`, `["code", code]` and `["summary"]`.

rules.message: Keep `summary()` memoised: cache its result in a field of the cart (such as `this.cache`, a version number or a dirty flag) instead of repricing on every call.

Rui sent this after reconciling September:

> The collected-by-partner report says Northwind paid us **$1,284.00** in September. Their remittances add up to **$942.00**. And Corvid isn't on the report at all. They're the one I need to chase: they haven't paid a cent since August.

Northwind moved its bigger customers onto two-part invoices in August, so some orders now have more than one payment, and some are only partly paid so far.

Fix the collected-by-partner query. It reads two tables:

| Table | Column | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `orders` | `id` | `integer`, primary key | the order |
| `orders` | `partner` | `text`, not null | the partner the order came through |
| `orders` | `total` | `numeric(12, 2)`, not null | what the order was invoiced for |
| `payments` | `id` | `integer`, primary key | the payment |
| `payments` | `order_id` | `integer`, not null, references `orders (id)` | the order it pays for |
| `payments` | `amount` | `numeric(12, 2)`, not null | the amount received |

An order can have no payments, one, or several, and its payments need not add up to its total.

The query returns one row per partner that has at least one order, with two columns:

1. `partner`;
2. `collected`: the sum of every payment received on that partner's orders, or `0` when none of them has been paid.

Rows are ordered by `collected`, biggest first; partners with the same amount are in alphabetical order, so the PDF doesn't reshuffle every month. With no orders the result has no rows.

queries/collected-by-partner.sql.text:
-- Finance's collected-by-partner report: what each partner's customers have paid us.
-- orders(id, partner, total), payments(id, order_id, amount)
SELECT o.partner, SUM(o.total) AS collected
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.partner
ORDER BY collected DESC;

rules.message: Every payment counts: two payments of the same amount are two payments, so don't add up only the distinct amounts.

Monday's import into the herbarium database created 14 "new" species that it already had. From the import log:

```text
new species: Carabus Nemoralis        (have: Carabus nemoralis)
new species: Carabus Sp.              (have: Carabus sp.)
new species: Pterostichus Niger       (have: Pterostichus niger)
```

The import matches species names exactly, so every name on the end-of-day tally sheet must be written the way the herbarium writes it.

`species_tally(lines)` takes the day's notebook lines (a list of strings) and returns a dict from species name to the total number of individuals of that species.

- A line reads `date | site | species | length | count`, for example `2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2`. `parse_line(line)` from `notebook.labels` (already imported) returns it as a dict with the keys `date`, `site`, `species` and `length` (strings, stripped of surrounding spaces) and `count` (an int).
- Lines that are empty or only whitespace are skipped.
- Each species is keyed by its herbarium name, which `canonical_name(name)` from `notebook.names` returns: it splits the name on whitespace, capitalises the first word (first letter upper case, the rest lower case), lowercases every other word, and joins the words with single spaces. `"  leistus   FERRUGINEUS "` becomes `"Leistus ferrugineus"`; a name with no words becomes `""`.
- Lines whose species have the same herbarium name are one species: their counts add up.
- Every species on a non-blank line is in the result, even when its total is 0. No lines gives `{}`.

Requirement: the names must come from `canonical_name` itself, not from a naming rule of your own, so the tally sheet and the herbarium can't drift apart again.

notebook/__init__.py.text: """The field notebook: specimen lots typed up from the paper notebook, and what we report on them."""

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

During a lockout the login form says when to try again. Today it rounds the time left down, so with 30 seconds left it says **"Too many attempts. Try again in 0 minutes."**, people retry straight away and lock themselves out again.

`retryMessage($secondsLeft)` takes the whole seconds left on the lock and returns the message. Lockouts run from one minute up to 24 hours.

- Round the time left **up**, so nobody is told to come back before the lock ends. Never round down: no `floor()` or `intdiv()`.
- Under 60 minutes (after rounding up), say minutes: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 minute.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.`
- From 60 minutes on, say hours, also rounded up: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 hour.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 2 hours.`
- Use the singular for exactly 1 minute or 1 hour, the plural otherwise.
- The lock can end between the check and the page render, so the seconds left can be zero or negative. Then the form says `You can try again now.`

{

}

Finance's September sales-tax filing came out $310.22 under the tax customers were actually charged. The filing is the sum of what `lineTaxes` returns for every order, and those line taxes don't add up to the order's tax. A receipt also charged tax on a gift card.

One order, at 8.25%, as the receipt shows it today:

```text
Order #20417                      net      tax
  Rain jacket                  $45.00    $3.71
  Tee × 2                      $45.00    $3.71
  Socks                        $10.80    $0.89
  Tax                                    $8.32   ← the lines add up to $8.31
```

Fix `receipt(order)` and `lineTaxes(amounts, rate)` so they follow Finance's rules. All amounts are whole cents; rates are basis points (825 is 8.25%).

**Input.** An `Order` is `{ id, taxRate, lines }`. Each line is `{ sku, price, quantity, discount, taxable }`: `price` is per unit, `discount` is the line's share of the order's promo code, and `taxable` is `false` for gift cards and donations.

**Output.** A `Receipt` is `{ lines, net, tax, total }`, where `lines` has one `{ sku, net, tax }` per order line, in order.

**Rules.**

- A line's `net` is `price × quantity − discount`. The receipt's `net` is the sum of every line's net, gift cards included.
- A line's taxable amount is its net when `taxable` is `true`, and 0 when it is `false`. A non-taxable line's tax is 0.
- The order is taxed once: the sum of the taxable amounts times the rate, divided by 10,000 and rounded half up to the cent. That is the receipt's `tax`, and `total` is `net + tax`.
- The line taxes add up to exactly the order's tax. Each line first gets its taxable amount times the rate, divided by 10,000 and rounded down. The cents still missing go one each to the lines with the largest remainders from that division; on a tie, the earlier line gets the cent first.
- `lineTaxes(amounts, rate)` takes the lines' taxable amounts in order and returns each line's tax by the rule above. Keep it exported with that signature (the finance export calls it with the taxable amounts) and take the receipt's line taxes from it.
- Keep money in whole cents: no `toFixed` or `parseFloat`.

`taxOn(amount, rate)` in the file is the tax on one amount, rounded half up to the cent.

rules.message: Keep the exported `lineTaxes(amounts, rate)`, returning each line's share of the order's tax, and take the receipt's line taxes from it: the finance export calls it too.
Keep money in whole cents: no `toFixed` or `parseFloat`.

Rui escalated Bluefin's October reconciliation:

> Bluefin's statement for 3 October says we're owed **€59.50** on 2 orders. Our settlement report says **€75.00** with **2 rejected rows**. Every night since 1 October has had rejected rows, always Bluefin's. Northwind still matches to the cent.

Bluefin's partner note from 28 September:

> From 1 October our settlement exports write negative amounts in accounting format: refunds and fees appear in brackets, e.g. `(12.50)`.

Their file for 3 October:

```text
partner,order_id,type,amount,currency
Bluefin,BF-77101,sale,45.00,EUR
Bluefin,BF-77102,sale,30.00,EUR
Bluefin,BF-77101,refund,(12.50),EUR
Bluefin,BF-FEE-10,adjustment,(3.00),EUR
```

`settlement_summary(text)` is what finance reconciles each partner's statement against. It takes a settlement export as CSV text, with the header `partner,order_id,type,amount,currency`, and returns `{"partners": [...], "rejected": n}`.

**Reading rows.** Each row of the export is read as follows. (In the starter, `read_settlements(text)` does the reading; only `settlement_summary`'s result is checked.)

- `partner` and `order` are trimmed; `currency` is trimmed and upper-cased.
- The type is trimmed and lower-cased, and must be `sale`, `refund` or `adjustment`; any other type rejects the row.
- An amount is read in whole cents. A plain amount is read by `to_cents(text)` from `pipeline.money` (already imported): a decimal number with an optional sign and at most two decimal places, with surrounding whitespace allowed (`"12.50"`, `"-3"`, `" 7.05 "`), becomes cents (`1250`, `-300`, `705`); anything else, including an empty string, `NaN` or more than two decimal places, raises `ValueError`. An amount in brackets, with surrounding whitespace allowed, is an accounting negative: `(12.50)` is `-1250`. What's inside the brackets must itself be a plain amount.
- A row whose amount can't be read is rejected: counted and left out, never guessed at. Only a bad type or a bad amount rejects a row; anything else wrong with the file (a missing column, say) is an error, not a rejected row.

**Summary.** One entry per partner and currency, as `{"partner", "currency", "sales", "refunds", "net"}`, sorted by partner and then currency:

- `sales` and `refunds` count the rows of each kind (adjustments aren't counted).
- `net` in cents is sales less refunds, plus adjustments (fees, corrections) with their own sign. A refund always reduces net by its size, whichever way the partner writes it: Northwind writes refunds as positive amounts, Bluefin in brackets.

`rejected` is the number of rejected rows, so nobody signs off on a partial file. A file with only the header gives `{"partners": [], "rejected": 0}`.

`count_words(text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

lib/count_words.rb.text:
# The number of words in a post, as the composer shows it under the text box.
def count_words(text)
  text.count(" ") + 1
end

Customers say password reset emails never work. They do, if you click within a minute: links expire far too early.

`isExpired($issuedAt, $now, $ttlMinutes)` returns whether a password reset link has expired. `$issuedAt` and `$now` are Unix timestamps in seconds, and `$ttlMinutes` is how long the link lasts, in minutes (0 or more).

- A link stays valid up to and including `$issuedAt + $ttlMinutes × 60`. It is expired only at a later time.

src/isExpired.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/**
 * Whether a password reset link has expired. Timestamps are Unix seconds;
 * a link stays valid until $issuedAt + $ttlMinutes * 60, inclusive.
 */
function isExpired(int $issuedAt, int $now, int $ttlMinutes): bool
{
    return $now > $issuedAt + $ttlMinutes;
}

The list endpoints accept any page size, and the mobile app sends `per_page=500` to fetch everything in one go. Cap it, don't reject it.

`ParsePage(query)` reads `page` and `per_page` from a URL query string without the leading `?`, such as `page=2&per_page=50`, and returns them as a `Page`.

- `page` defaults to 1 and `per_page` to 20.
- Each falls back to its default on its own when it is missing, empty, zero, negative or not a whole number.
- A `per_page` above 100 becomes 100. `page` has no upper limit.
- Parameter names are matched exactly, other parameters are ignored, and the order of parameters doesn't matter.

The volunteers typing up the 2026 notebooks are expanding every ditto mark by hand, and it's slow: three of 41 notebooks done. From Marta, who leads the fieldwork:

> We've always written " under the row above when nothing changed. Some of the older volunteers write 〃 or do. Please let them type the page as it looks.

`read_notebook(text)` reads a typed-up notebook (one string, lines separated by newlines) and returns `{"rows": [...], "unresolved": [...]}`.

**Lines.** A specimen row reads `date | site | species | length | count`, for example `2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2`. Three kinds of line are not specimen rows: blank lines (empty or only whitespace), notes (starting with `#` once leading spaces are removed), and page headings (starting with `==`, for example `== p. 14 ==`).

**Rows.** Each specimen row becomes a dict with the keys `date`, `site`, `species` and `length` (strings, stripped of surrounding spaces) and `count` (an int), in the order the rows appear. `notebook.labels` (already used by the starter) provides:

- `parse_line(line)`: that dict for one line, with no ditto expansion;
- `fields(line)`: the line's five fields as a list of stripped strings, in that order (raises `ValueError` if there aren't five);
- `FIELDS`: the field names, `("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")`.

**Ditto marks.**

- A field that is exactly `"`, `〃` or `do.` once stripped is a ditto. A field that only contains one of them among other text is not.
- A ditto means the same field as the nearest specimen row above it on the same page, as that row reads once its own dittos are expanded. This applies to every field, the count included.
- Blank lines and notes are skipped and are never the row above.
- A page heading starts a new sheet of paper: a ditto never reaches back across it. The first row after a heading has no row above.
- A ditto with nothing to copy (no row above, or the field above was itself a ditto with nothing to copy) can't be resolved. Its row can't be read: it is left out of `rows`, and its line number goes in `unresolved`. It still counts as the row above for the next row, whose dittos copy the fields it had and can't resolve the ones it didn't.
- Line numbers start at 1 and count every line of the text, including blank lines, notes and headings, so they match the line numbers in the volunteer's editor. `unresolved` lists them in order.

Empty text gives `{"rows": [], "unresolved": []}`.

Requirement: the code must not print anything. The transcription job's standard output goes into the volunteers' upload log.

notebook/__init__.py.text: """The field notebook: specimen lots typed up from the paper notebook, and what we report on them."""

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

Alerting is blind to the 502s: the access log parser comes back with empty fields.

`ParseLine(line)` parses one access log line, such as `GET /cart 200 12ms`, into an `Entry`. A line has four fields separated by single spaces:

- `Method`: the HTTP method, as written.
- `Path`: the request path as written, including any query string. It never contains a space.
- `Status`: the status code, as an integer.
- `Ms`: the duration, as an integer. Durations are always whole milliseconds followed by `ms`: `1300ms` is `1300`.

The edge proxy keeps the most recent request latencies in memory, in a fixed-size ring buffer that overwrites its oldest entry when it is full.

`ring_buffer(capacity, values, count, out)` pushes the `count` integers in `values`, in order, into an empty buffer that holds `capacity` entries. A push into a full buffer overwrites the oldest entry. Then it writes what the buffer holds into `out`, oldest first, and returns how many entries it wrote.

- `out` has room for at least `count` integers.
- A capacity of 0 holds nothing.

Since the cart moved to integer cents, the cart drawer shows amounts the way the API stores them. From a support ticket:

> My cart says the sofa costs **129900**. Is that dollars?? And my refund line says **-500**.

`formatPrice(cents)` takes an amount as a whole number of cents and returns the text the drawer, the receipts and the refund lines show.

- Show a dollar sign, then the whole dollars with a comma between every group of three digits, then a dot and exactly two digits of cents: `123456` → `"$1,234.56"`, `5` → `"$0.05"`.
- Negative amounts are refunds. The minus goes before the dollar sign, as on the receipts: `-500` → `"-$5.00"`.
- Amounts can run into the billions of cents.

sha256:750d33c31b99cc0d5626396bd6ef15b19.body:
Support escalated this from the help desk:

> A customer returned one of two jackets from an order that used **SPRING10** (10% off). The receipt says they paid **$45.00** for that jacket, but the refund came through as **$40.50**.

```text
Order #10482    SPRING10 (10% off)
  Rain jacket    1 × $50.00    −$5.00    $45.00
Refund #R-2291
  Rain jacket    1 × $50.00              −$40.50
```

`refundTotal(refund)` works out what a refund gives back. A refund must give back exactly what the customer paid for the lines returned.

**Input.** All amounts are whole cents, never floats. `refund` is `{ code, lines }`:

- `code` is the order's promo code: `null`, a percentage such as `{ percent: 10 }`, or a fixed amount in cents such as `{ amount: 500 }`.
- `lines` are the returned order lines, each `{ sku, price, quantity, discount }`. `price` is the unit price. `discount` is the part of the order's discount that checkout took off this line: at checkout the code's discount is spread over all the order's lines in proportion to their value and stored on each line.

**Output.** What the customer paid for the returned lines, as a negative number of cents: refunds stay negative all the way to the ledger. When they paid nothing for them, it is `0`.

**What the file imports.** These helpers can't be changed:

- `lineTotal(line)` from `./money.js`: what a line charged, `price × quantity − discount` (a missing `discount` counts as 0).
- `sum(amounts)` from `./money.js`: the sum of a list of amounts, `0` for an empty list.
- `discountFor(code, subtotal)` from `./discounts.js`: a code's discount on a subtotal: `0` without a code, `Math.round(subtotal × percent / 100)` for a percentage, `amount` for a fixed amount, and never more than `subtotal`.

**Leave `orderTotal` as it is.** Checkout uses it, and it must keep taking the code's discount (`discountFor(order.code, …)`) off the order's subtotal. Keep the change to refunds.

`WordCount.Count(text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

Customers keep emailing about a one-cent difference between the invoice and the reminder: the late fee doesn't round the way finance's spreadsheet does.

`LateFee(balance, daysLate)` returns the late fee on an overdue invoice. `balance` is the amount owed in dollars (0 or more, to the cent), and the fee is in dollars too.

- The fee is 0.5% of the balance for each day late, at most 10% of the balance.
- That fee is rounded to cents with halves rounded away from zero, as the spreadsheet does: a fee of 0.505 is 0.51.
- Nothing is charged when `daysLate` is 0 or negative.

The category page's filter form has two checkboxes, `in-stock` and `on-sale`, with bare text next to them. The accessibility audit flagged them: screen readers announce "checkbox" and nothing else, and clicking the text does not toggle the box.

Tie each checkbox to a label:

- Give each checkbox the id `filter-NAME`, where NAME is its `name`: `filter-in-stock` and `filter-on-sale`.
- Give each checkbox a `<label for="filter-NAME">` whose text is exactly its name.
- Keep both checkboxes, in the same order, with their `type` and `name` attributes, and keep everything inside the one `<form>`. The page has no other checkboxes or labels.

Each check runs a CSS selector against the page and reads something from the matching elements, in document order: their `count`, their `text`, their accessible `label`, or an attribute such as `name` or `id`.

Security raised the minimum password length to 12, and the sign-up form says 12, but the API still checks 8 and reports no other rule.

`PasswordPolicy.violations(password)` returns every rule the password breaks, in this order:

1. `"too-short"`: fewer than 12 characters. Every character counts, whitespace included.
2. `"no-digit"`: no digit.
3. `"no-letter"`: no letter, in either case.
4. `"has-whitespace"`: a space, tab or other whitespace character anywhere.

A password that breaks none of them gets an empty list.

sha256:9714f502ad5ae2dbc1a23b5b57f736398.body:
Last week's change to session refresh (#412) added a grace window so the mobile app stops logging people out when two screens refresh at the same moment. The logouts stopped, but the `refresh_reuse` alert, about 40 a day before, has not fired since, and a pentest exchanged a refresh token captured on Oct 20 for a fresh one on Oct 23 while the victim's session stayed alive.

`refresh(family, presented, now)` decides one refresh. Find everything #412 broke against the rules below and fix it. Keep the grace window: the mobile fix has to stay. `refresh` is pure: the caller stores whatever it decides. Times are Unix milliseconds.

**Sessions.** A login starts a session family. A client refreshes with the family's current refresh token and gets the next one; each refresh token works once.

- `family` is `{ id, userId, loginAt, revoked, tokens }`. `tokens` lists the family's refresh tokens oldest first, and the last is the current one. Each is `{ token, issuedAt, rotatedAt }`, where `rotatedAt` is when it was exchanged for the next token, or `null` while it is current.
- `presented` is the token string the client sent; `now` is the time of the request.

**The rules, in this order** (the first that applies decides):

1. A token that is not in the family: `{ status: "reauth", reason: "unknown", revokeFamily: false }`.
2. A revoked family (signed out everywhere, password changed): `{ status: "reauth", reason: "revoked", revokeFamily: false }`.
3. A family `SESSION_LIFETIME_MS` (30 days) or more after its `loginAt`: `{ status: "reauth", reason: "expired", revokeFamily: false }`.
4. A token that was already rotated (`rotatedAt` is not `null`):
   - up to `REFRESH_GRACE_MS` (10 seconds) after that token's own rotation, inclusive, the client lost a race with itself: `{ status: "ok", token }` with the family's current token, and nothing new is issued;
   - any later, someone else has a copy: `{ status: "reauth", reason: "reuse", revokeFamily: true }`.
5. Otherwise rotate: `{ status: "ok", token }` with the family's next token, `${family.id}.${tokens.length + 1}`.

Only "reuse" revokes the family (`revokeFamily: true`).

**Code the file imports.** From `./policy`: `SESSION_LIFETIME_MS` (30 days) and `REFRESH_GRACE_MS` (10,000). From `./tokens`: `findToken(family, presented)` returns the family's token with that string, or `undefined`; `current(family)` returns the family's last token; `nextToken(family)` returns the string a rotation issues, as in rule 5; and the types `SessionFamily` and `RefreshResult`.

**Requirements.**

- Keep the grace window, measured with `REFRESH_GRACE_MS`.
- No console logging (`console.log`, `info`, `debug`, `warn` or `error`): the gateway's output is searchable company-wide, and must never sit next to a refresh token.

src/gateway/policy.ts.text:
/**
 * Session rules for the login gateway, as signed off by security (SEC-118).
 *
 * A login starts a session family. A client refreshes with the family's current refresh token
 * and gets the next one; each refresh token works once. A refresh is decided in this order:
 *
 *   1. A token that is not in the family: sign in again ("unknown").
 *   2. A revoked family (signed out everywhere, password changed): sign in again ("revoked").
 *   3. A family SESSION_LIFETIME_MS or more after its login: sign in again ("expired").
 *   4. A token that was already rotated:
 *      - up to REFRESH_GRACE_MS after its rotation (inclusive), the client lost a race with
 *        itself: answer with the family's current token and issue nothing new;
 *      - any later, someone else has a copy: sign in again ("reuse") and revoke the family.
 *   5. Otherwise rotate: issue the family's next token.
 *
 * Only "reuse" revokes the family: every token in it stops working, the current one included.
 */

/** Mobile sessions last 30 days from login, however often they refresh. */
export const SESSION_LIFETIME_MS = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

/** How long a just-rotated token is still answered, for clients that refresh twice at once. */
export const REFRESH_GRACE_MS = 10 * 1000;

rules.message: Keep the grace window for a just-rotated token, measured with `REFRESH_GRACE_MS`.
No console logging in the gateway: no `console.log`, `info`, `debug`, `warn` or `error`.

sha256:9d9b6ceecbb1e6e13ea0296425ab6f627.body:
We want to start the origin-v2 canary on Monday at 10% of traffic. The upstream block already says so:

```text
upstream origin {
    server origin-v1 weight=9;
    server origin-v2 weight=1;
}
```

but the balancer never looks at weights. In staging last night origin-v2 got **10,041 of 20,000** requests (50.2%).

Each `server <name> weight=<n>;` line is already parsed into a `Backend` (`Name`, `Weight`). The proxy calls `RoundRobin.Next` once per request; `PickOrder(backends, n)` returns where the next `n` requests go on a freshly loaded upstream (a new `RoundRobin` over `backends`), for previews before a rollout. Make the balancer honour weights.

## Rules

- A server with weight `n` gets `n` shares of the upstream's requests, spread out rather than in bursts (smooth weighted round robin, as nginx does it).
- `weight=0` drains a server: it keeps its place in the list but gets no requests and takes no part in the calculation below.
- With no servers, or every server drained, there is nowhere to send a request: `Next` returns `false` and `PickOrder` returns no picks (an empty list). `PickOrder` with `n = 0` also returns an empty list.
- Otherwise `PickOrder` returns exactly `n` server names, in order.

## The algorithm

1. Every server starts with a current value of 0.
2. For each request, add each non-drained server's weight to its current value.
3. Pick the server with the highest current value; on a tie, the one listed first.
4. Subtract the total weight of all non-drained servers from the picked server's current value.

Worked example with weights a=5, b=1, c=1 (total 7):

| Request | After adding weights (a, b, c) | Picked | After subtracting 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5, 1, 1 | a | -2, 1, 1 |
| 2 | 3, 2, 2 | a | -4, 2, 2 |
| 3 | 1, 3, 3 | b | 1, -4, 3 |
| 4 | 6, -3, 4 | a | -1, -3, 4 |
| 5 | 4, -2, 5 | c | 4, -2, -2 |
| 6 | 9, -1, -1 | a | 2, -1, -1 |
| 7 | 7, 0, 0 | a | 0, 0, 0 |

## Constraints

- `Next` is called concurrently from every connection's goroutine and now updates shared state on each call: it must keep locking `r.mu` while it reads and updates that state.

rules.message: RoundRobin.Next is called concurrently from every connection's goroutine, so it must lock r.mu while it reads and updates the balancer's state.

The cache's hit rate dropped to 12% after the last deploy: entries that were just read get evicted.

`simulate(capacity, ops)` runs `ops` in order against an empty least-recently-used (LRU) cache that holds at most `capacity` entries (at least 1), and returns the result of each get, in order.

- `["put", key, value]` stores `value` under `key`. If the key is already cached, its value is replaced. If the key is new and the cache is full, the least recently used entry is evicted first.
- `["get", key]` returns the key's value, or `-1` when it isn't cached.
- A put and a get that finds its key both count as a use, making that key the most recently used. A get that misses changes nothing.

Workspace URLs are `/w/<slug>`. For names with accents, the link we email is percent-encoded and 404s.

`slugify(name)` turns a workspace name into its slug:

- The slug has only lowercase ASCII letters `a`–`z`, digits `0`–`9` and hyphens. Uppercase letters become lowercase.
- Accented Latin letters lose their accents and keep their base letter, whether the accent is part of the character or a separate combining mark after it: `"Café Ünïcorn"` → `"cafe-unicorn"`.
- Every run of anything else (spaces, punctuation, underscores, hyphens, symbols, emoji, other scripts) between kept characters becomes a single hyphen. There is no hyphen at either end.
- A name with nothing to keep gives `""`.

# Workspace URLs are /w/<slug>. Turn a workspace name into its slug:
# lowercase ASCII letters and digits, words joined by single hyphens.
def slugify(name)
  name.downcase.tr(" ", "-")
end

A credential-stuffing bot hit the login endpoint again last night. Limit login attempts with a sliding window.

`allow(times, limit, windowMs)` gets the times of login attempts in milliseconds, in order (several can share a time), and returns, for each attempt, whether it is allowed.

- An attempt at time `t` is allowed when fewer than `limit` allowed attempts fall in the window from just after `t − windowMs` up to and including `t`. Otherwise it is rejected.
- Rejected attempts don't count toward the limit.
- `limit` can be 0, which rejects every attempt.

sha256:c4e014d80b90e5c32a44fb2579ab421aa.body:
Since the IPv6 listener went live on Tuesday, every request that addresses the proxy by its v6 literal gets the default vhost's **421 Misdirected Request**. The health checker on `[2001:db8::1]:8080` has been red since; on-call silenced it at 02:10.

```text
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/healthz host="[2001" vhost=default
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]/healthz      host="["     vhost=default
```

The proxy routes each request on its Host header after `normalize_host` has normalized it, and the response cache keys on the same value, so two spellings of one host share a vhost and cache entries. Plain hostnames already work; IPv6 literals do not, because the current code treats the first `:` as the start of the port.

## What to write

`int normalize_host(const char *host, char *out, size_t size)`

- `host` is the raw Host header value, a NUL-terminated string.
- Write the normalized host into `out`, NUL-terminated, and return its length (not counting the terminator).
- `size` is the size of `out` in bytes, terminator included. If the result plus its terminator does not fit, return `-1`.
- Return `-1` when the value is not a host. The examples show `-1` as `null`, and a string for a host.

## Normalizing rules

- **Port:** remove the port. For a hostname, the port is everything from the first `:` on (`example.com:8443` becomes `example.com`).
- **IPv6 literals:** a value starting with `[` is an IPv6 literal. It keeps its brackets and loses only a port after the closing `]` (`[2001:db8::1]:8080` becomes `[2001:db8::1]`). A literal that is never closed with `]`, or whose `]` is followed by anything other than nothing or a `:` port, is not a host.
- **Trailing dot:** after the port is removed, a single trailing `.` is removed (`cdn.example.com.` becomes `cdn.example.com`).
- **Case:** ASCII letters are lowercased, in hostnames and IPv6 literals alike (`Example.COM` becomes `example.com`).
- **Empty:** a value with nothing left after these steps is not a host.

Plain hostnames must keep normalizing exactly as they do now.

## Constraints

- No heap allocation: `normalize_host` runs on every request before routing, and `out` is the buffer to write into. Do not call `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `strdup` or `strndup`.

rules.message: normalize_host must not allocate on the heap (no malloc, calloc, realloc, strdup or strndup): write the result into out.

"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

notebook/sites.py.text:
"""Per-site totals for the season summary."""
from itertools import groupby

from notebook.labels import parse_line


def site_summary(lines):
    """Per site: lots, individuals, distinct species, and the first and last date it was
    visited."""
    # One pass instead of rescanning the notebook for every site: the export is in notebook
    # order, so each site's lines come together.
    rows = [parse_line(line) for line in lines]
    summary = {}
    for site, group in groupby(rows, key=lambda row: row["site"]):
        group = list(group)
        summary[site] = {
            "lots": len(group),
            "individuals": sum(row["count"] for row in group),
            "species": len({row["species"] for row in group}),
            "first": group[0]["date"],
            "last": group[-1]["date"],
        }
    return summary

rules.message: Don't go over all the lines once for each site: the summary has to stay fast on a 40,000-line export.

Timeouts in config must be written in seconds, and somebody set `idle_timeout = 3600` meaning minutes. Let people write `1h`.

`ParseDuration(text)` turns a duration such as `"1h30m"`, `"45s"` or `"2h"` into seconds, or returns an error when the text isn't a valid duration (the checks show an error as `null`).

- A valid duration is one or more parts written together, each a whole number in digits followed by a unit: `h` (hours), `m` (minutes) or `s` (seconds).
- Each unit appears at most once, in the order `h`, `m`, `s`, and any of them can be left out. A number can be 0 and can be larger than the next unit up.
- Anything else is an error: for example an empty string, a number without a unit, a unit without a number, any other unit or an uppercase one, a sign, a decimal point, spaces, or units repeated or out of order.

Rui, first thing Monday:

> Monday's active-customers report says **18,406**. Last Monday it was **18,618**, and nobody closed 212 accounts over the weekend. I spot-checked three of the missing ones and they're all phone orders from the Leeds store:

```text
id       name               email   phone
C-20931  Hollis Bakery              0113 496 0021
C-20977  Marsh & Daughters          0113 496 0088
C-21012  T. Okafor                  0113 496 0140
```

The dedupe step was sped up on Tuesday: it used to compare every pair of records, which took 40 minutes on Northwind's 180k-row file, and now it makes one pass with a dict. This is the first Monday report since.

`dedupe_customers(rows)` takes the night's customer records (a list of dicts, each with fields such as `id`, `name`, `email` and `phone`; a field's value may be `None`) and returns one record per customer, in the order customers were first seen.

- Records whose emails match once normalised are the same customer. `normalize_email(email)` from `pipeline.normalize` (already imported) does the normalising: it returns the email trimmed of surrounding whitespace and lowercased, or `None` when there is no usable email (`None`, empty, or only whitespace). Phone and in-store customers often have none.
- For each customer, the first record is kept. A later duplicate only fills in fields the kept record left blank (`None` or `""`, or missing): each such field takes the duplicate's value, so the earliest later duplicate with a value wins. Nothing else changes; in particular the kept record's email stays as written.
- A record without a usable email can't be matched to anything, so it is always kept, as it is, in its place.
- The input rows (and their dicts) must not be changed. No rows gives `[]`.

The starter's `_fill_blanks(customer, duplicate)` already fills a kept record's blank fields from a duplicate, in place.

Requirement: keep it to one pass with a lookup by email. Don't compare each record against the customers kept so far: the nightly window is two hours.

"""Normalising fields before records are compared or loaded."""


def normalize_email(email):
    """An email as we compare it: trimmed and lowercased.

    None when there is no usable email on file (missing, empty or only spaces): phone and
    in-store customers often have none.
    """
    if email is None:
        return None
    email = email.strip().lower()
    return email or None

The season report fails as soon as it reaches the sheets from the Oregon volunteers:

```text
  File "notebook/report.py", line 10, in to_mm
    return float(value) * MM_PER[unit]
KeyError: 'in'
```

Their sheets differ from ours: lengths can be in inches (`0.6 in`), sometimes with no space before the unit or with the unit in capitals (`12mm`, `1.3 CM`, `0.5in`), and lots nobody measured have the length left blank, or a `?` when the volunteer wasn't sure. We take the sheets the way the volunteers write them.

`length_report(lines)` takes the season's notebook lines (a list of strings, one specimen lot each) and returns a dict keyed by species name, exactly as written on the line. For each species:

- `measured`: how many of its lots have a length. Each lot counts once, whatever its individual count.
- `min_mm`, `max_mm`, `mean_mm`: the shortest, longest and mean of those lengths in millimetres, each rounded to one decimal (the mean is taken over the unrounded lengths).

A line reads `date | site | species | length | count`, for example `2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2`. `parse_line(line)` from `notebook.labels` (already imported) returns it as a dict with the keys `date`, `site`, `species` and `length` (strings, stripped of surrounding spaces) and `count` (an int).

A length is a number (digits, optionally with a decimal part), then any amount of space or none, then a unit: `mm`, `cm` (10 mm) or `in` (25.4 mm), in any mix of upper and lower case. A blank length or `?` means the lot wasn't measured: it doesn't count towards any of the numbers, but its species still appears. A species with no measured lot shows `measured: 0` and `None` for the three lengths. No lines gives `{}`.

notebook/__init__.py.text: """The field notebook: specimen lots typed up from the paper notebook, and what we report on them."""

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

Sign-up compares email addresses exactly as typed, so someone who signed up as `Jane.Doe@Example.com` and signs up again as `jane.doe@example.com ` gets a second account. Write the key sign-up looks accounts up by, so one person gets one account however they type their address. (The address itself is still stored exactly as typed; this is only the lookup key.)

`CanonicalEmail(raw)` returns the key and `ok` true, or `""` and `ok` false for anything that is not an address we accept:

- Surrounding whitespace is ignored. Whitespace anywhere inside the address (spaces, tabs, any Unicode space) makes it invalid.
- An address has exactly one `@`, with something on both sides of it.
- The whole address is lowercased: every provider our users are on treats the local part case-insensitively.
- For **gmail.com** and **googlemail.com** (those exact domains after lowercasing; not their subdomains or longer domains), dots in the local part are dropped, so is everything from the first `+` on, and the domain becomes `gmail.com`. Other domains keep their dots and `+` tags as they are: plenty of mail servers deliver `+` addresses to different people.
- If the Gmail rules leave the local part empty, the address is invalid.

`count_words(text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

Customers type promo codes the way they read them in the email, and checkout rejects codes typed in lowercase or with stray spaces.

`applyDiscount(totalCents, code, codes)` returns an order's total after its promo code's discount.

- `totalCents` is the total in whole cents. `code` is what the customer typed. `codes` maps each configured code to its percent off, from 0 to 100: `{ SAVE10: 10 }`.
- The typed code matches a configured code when the two are equal ignoring letter case and ignoring spaces before and after the typed code. Spaces inside a code still count, and configured codes may be written in any case. Only codes in `codes` match.
- With a match, return the total less that percentage, rounded down to whole cents.
- Without a match, including an empty or blank code, return the total unchanged.

sha256:f98317c26bb64445f4653825150a3f91e.body:
Kettlebrook's checkout has been failing since Thursday's release, which shipped CHK-412 (free shipping from $30 for loyalty members). Every customer checking out as a guest gets "Something went wrong" on the payment page instead of a quote: `POST /quote` returns 500 with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'tier')` thrown in `quoteOrder`. Members' orders still get quotes. For example, guest order #88213 (two stoneware mugs at $18.00 each) failed.

Fix `quoteOrder` so that every order gets a correct quote.

## Input and output

`quoteOrder(order)` takes an order and returns `{ subtotal, shipping, total }`, all whole cents (never floats); the payment page charges exactly that.

- `order.items` is a list of `{ sku, price, quantity }`, with `price` in cents. `subtotal` is the sum of `price × quantity` over the items.
- `order.customer` is either a guest, `{ guest: true }`, which has no loyalty record at all, or a member, `{ id, loyalty: { tier } }`, where `tier` is a string such as `"silver"`, `"gold"` or `"none"`.
- `total` is `subtotal + shipping`.

## Shipping rules

- Standard shipping is $4.95 (495 cents).
- Shipping is free for everyone when the subtotal is $50.00 (5000 cents) or more.
- A loyalty member gets free shipping when the subtotal is $30.00 (3000 cents) or more. A loyalty member is a customer with a loyalty record whose tier is not `"none"`.
- A guest is not a loyalty member. A member whose tier is `"none"` has lapsed and is not a loyalty member either: both get the standard $50 threshold.

## Code you can use

The starter imports these; their code is fixed and you cannot change it:

- `lineTotal(item)` returns `item.price * item.quantity`; `sum(amounts)` adds a list of numbers (0 for an empty list).
- `shippingFor(subtotal, member)` returns the shipping in cents under the rules above: 0 when `subtotal` is at least 3000 if `member` is `true`, or at least 5000 if it is `false`; 495 otherwise. The module also exports the constants `SHIPPING` (495), `FREE_FROM` (5000) and `MEMBER_FREE_FROM` (3000).

## Constraints

- Handle guests and lapsed members explicitly. Do not use `catch` (no `try`/`catch` and no `.catch(`): catching the error would turn the crash into a silently wrong quote.
